title: Visuospatial Neglect - a Theory-Informed Overview of Current and Emerging Strategies and a Systematic Review on the Therapeutic Use of Non-invasive Brain Stimulation

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Definition of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Definition and Core Clinical Features of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect (VSN) is a neuropsychological syndrome characterized by a failure to attend to, report, or respond to stimuli located in the contralesional space, most commonly the left hemispace following right hemisphere brain damage. It is not a primary sensory or motor deficit but rather a disorder of spatial attention and awareness, often manifesting as an ipsilesional bias in orienting and exploration. Core clinical features include inattention to contralateral visual, auditory, and somatosensory stimuli, as well as neglect of personal space (e.g., ignoring the left side of the body during grooming) and extrapersonal space (e.g., omitting left-side items in cancellation tasks). Patients frequently lack awareness of their deficit (anosognosia), which complicates rehabilitation and prognosis ref [5].

Importantly, VSN can dissociate into distinct subtypes: egocentric (viewer-centered) neglect, allocentric (object-centered) neglect, representational neglect (impaired mental imagery of contralesional space), and motor neglect (reduced initiation of movements toward the neglected side) ref [12]. Representational neglect, for instance, may persist even in the absence of perceptual deficits, as demonstrated in patients who fail to describe the left side of familiar landmarks in mental imagery despite intact visual perception ref [16]. Recent evidence further reveals that neglect can extend to non-visual domains, such as the mental number line, where patients exhibit spatially biased numerical bisection errors independent of perceptual input ref [15]. These dissociations underscore the heterogeneity of VSN and its multifactorial origins, necessitating multimodal assessment for accurate diagnosis ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Definition of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect arises from a distributed network of cortical and subcortical structures, primarily in the right hemisphere. Core cortical regions consistently implicated include the inferior parietal lobule—particularly the supramarginal and angular gyri—as well as the frontal eye field and middle/inferior frontal gyri, which together support attentional orienting and spatial representation ref [5]. Recent evidence highlights that neglect is not solely a cortical phenomenon; subcortical structures such as the putamen, pulvinar, and caudate nucleus are also critical, forming a cortico-subcortical circuit with the superior temporal gyrus that modulates spatial awareness ref [9].

Importantly, white matter disconnection plays a pivotal role, with damage to the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), particularly its posterior segment, strongly associated with persistent neglect, even in the absence of cortical infarction or hemianopia ref [8]. Virtual tractography studies confirm that disruption of parietal-frontal pathways, rather than gray matter lesions alone, predicts the severity and chronicity of neglect ref [5]. Furthermore, perfusion imaging in acute stroke reveals that functional hypoperfusion of the superior temporal gyrus underlies allocentric neglect, while angular gyrus hypoperfusion correlates with egocentric neglect, suggesting distinct neural substrates for subtypes ref [6].

A meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation corroborates these findings, identifying consistent lesion clusters in the middle and superior temporal gyrus, intraparietal sulcus, precuneus, and posterior insula, alongside white matter tracts connecting these regions ref [12]. Collectively, these data support a network-based model of neglect, wherein dysfunction arises from both focal gray matter damage and widespread white matter disconnection, challenging the traditional view of neglect as a purely parietal disorder ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Definition of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Subtypes and Dissociations: Representational, Motor, and Non-Spatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect manifests in distinct subtypes that dissociate based on the cognitive or motor systems affected. Representational neglect, characterized by failure to attend to contralesional space in mental imagery, can occur independently of perceptual neglect. For instance, a patient with a right thalamic lesion exhibited pure representational neglect, omitting left-sided details in mental images of familiar scenes despite intact perceptual processing, suggesting distinct neural substrates for imagined versus perceived space ref [11]. Further evidence supports dissociable representations: patients often neglect the left side of imagined city squares but not the left side of imagined clocks, indicating that topological (environmental) and non-topological (object-based) mental representations may be differentially vulnerable ref [12].

Motor neglect, distinct from sensory or primary motor deficits, involves reduced initiation or utilization of contralesional limbs, particularly during bimanual tasks. A case study demonstrated that a patient with motor neglect performed normally in unimanual reaches but showed severe impairment in contralesional movements during bimanual actions, with performance modulated by visual grouping of targets—suggesting a late-stage attentional bias in motor competition ref [10]. This form of motor extinction highlights the role of interlimb coordination networks and competitive action selection mechanisms. Non-spatial neglect, though less commonly discussed, encompasses deficits in attention to non-spatial features (e.g., number magnitude, time) and may arise from disruptions in attentional networks beyond the spatial domain, often co-occurring with spatial neglect but potentially dissociable in its neural basis ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Epidemiology, Frequency, and Prognostic Impact of Neglect After Stroke
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is a highly prevalent disorder following stroke, particularly after right hemisphere lesions. Large cohort studies report an incidence of approximately 43% in acute right-brain-lesioned patients, compared to only 20% in left-brain-lesioned patients, highlighting a strong hemispheric asymmetry ref [14]. This frequency declines over time, with persistent neglect observed in 17% of right-hemisphere stroke patients at 3 months post-onset, versus 5% in left-hemisphere patients ref [14]. The severity and persistence of neglect are strongly associated with cortical, particularly right temporoparietal, lesions, while subcortical involvement confers a lower risk ref [14]. Age is a significant risk factor, with older patients showing higher rates of neglect, especially after right-hemisphere injury, whereas gender and handedness show minimal influence ref [14].

The prognostic impact of neglect is substantial and independent of motor deficits. Studies demonstrate that the severity of unilateral spatial neglect, as measured by behavioral inattention tests, is a robust predictor of functional outcomes during inpatient rehabilitation, including lower gains in activities of daily living, reduced FIM efficiency, and diminished rehabilitation effectiveness ref [16]. Furthermore, subtypes of neglect—particularly peripersonal and extrapersonal spatial deficits—are associated with greater functional impairment than neglect confined to personal space, with up to 69% of neglect patients showing peripersonal involvement ref [17]. Longitudinal analyses confirm that perceptual-attentional deficits, rather than motor components, are the most persistent and predictive of long-term disability ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Introduction and Definition of Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.subsection_title: Attentional and Arousal Mechanisms Underlying Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is increasingly understood as a disorder of attentional and arousal systems rather than a purely spatial deficit. The right hemisphere hosts a distributed network that integrates sensory, motivational, and arousal components to sustain directed attention across both hemispaces. Mesulam’s model posits that the reticular formation provides the foundational level of arousal necessary for spatial orienting, and its disruption contributes to the persistent inattention characteristic of neglect ref [21]. This is corroborated by evidence that diminished general alertness exacerbates spatial bias, while interventions that enhance arousal—such as auditory stimuli or pharmacological agents—can transiently ameliorate neglect symptoms ref [19].

Critically, recent work demonstrates that even endogenous, cognitive manipulations—such as inducing perceived time-pressure—can modulate alertness and reduce neglect severity without external stimulation, suggesting intact top-down control over arousal networks despite structural damage ref [19]. Furthermore, nonlateralized attentional deficits, including reduced vigilance and impaired sustained attention independent of spatial location, are prevalent in chronic neglect and may underlie its persistence beyond spatial mapping errors ref [18]. Neuroimaging studies confirm that neglect correlates with dysfunction in both ventral and dorsal attention networks, with ventral lesions disrupting target detection and reorienting, while simultaneously impairing the functional connectivity of dorsal networks responsible for spatial selection ref [13].

Structural analyses from the Sunnybrook Stroke Study reveal that damage to parietal and anterior cingulate regions, along with white matter tracts connecting frontal and parietal areas, strongly predicts both the severity of neglect and associated arousal deficits, highlighting the interdependence of attentional control and vigilance systems ref [15]. Together, these findings support a network-based model in which neglect arises from the failure of integrated attentional and arousal mechanisms, rather than isolated spatial representation deficits.

subsections.subsection_title: Subtype Heterogeneity and Temporal Stability of Neglect Presentation
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect exhibits marked subtype heterogeneity, commonly categorized into perceptual, motor, and personal neglect, with emerging evidence suggesting these subtypes may reflect distinct neurocognitive mechanisms. However, the temporal stability of these subtypes remains contentious. A seminal study by Hamilton et al. demonstrated that 85.7% of acute stroke patients with neglect exhibited changes in subtype expression across three testing sessions, with 61.9% showing inconsistencies not attributable to general recovery, challenging the assumption of stable subtype classification ref [23]. This variability suggests that single-timepoint assessments may misclassify neglect profiles, potentially undermining subtype-targeted interventions.

Further longitudinal studies corroborate this instability, revealing that while initial presentations often involve comorbid subtypes, symptom profiles tend to differentiate over time, becoming more discrete as recovery progresses ref [23]. Additional work by Doricchi et al. highlights that neglect subtypes may dynamically interact with attentional networks, leading to fluctuating expression depending on task demands and cognitive load ref [2]. Similarly, Chechlacz et al. found that lesion location alone cannot reliably predict subtype persistence, as functional reorganization and interhemispheric imbalance contribute to temporal shifts in symptom manifestation ref [3]. These findings collectively argue against rigid subtype taxonomies and underscore the need for repeated, multimodal assessment across the recovery trajectory to inform prognosis and personalize rehabilitation strategies.

subsections.subsection_title: Guidelines and Standardization in Neglect Assessment
subsections.content:
Standardization in the assessment of visuospatial neglect remains a critical challenge due to the heterogeneity of clinical presentations and the lack of universally adopted protocols. Major clinical guidelines, including those from the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association, emphasize the importance of routine neglect screening in acute stroke settings to guide rehabilitation planning and predict functional outcomes ref [24]. Despite this, variability persists in the choice of assessment tools across institutions, with some centers relying on single-screening tasks (e.g., line bisection or cancellation) while others employ comprehensive batteries. Efforts to harmonize assessment have been advanced by expert consensus statements advocating for the integration of multiple modalities—such as paper-and-pencil tests, behavioral observations, and functional tasks—to capture the multidimensional nature of neglect ref [2]. The European Stroke Organization and the International Society for Neurorehabilitation have similarly called for standardized, time-efficient protocols suitable for diverse clinical environments, particularly in acute care and rehabilitation units. However, implementation gaps remain, partly due to insufficient training and resource limitations. Emerging frameworks propose digital and tablet-based assessments to improve reliability and objectivity, yet these require further validation in multicenter trials. Consensus on core outcome measures and reporting standards is urgently needed to facilitate cross-study comparisons and evidence-based practice.

To address these challenges, recent initiatives have promoted the adoption of a minimum data set for neglect assessment, including tasks that evaluate perceptual, motor, and representational components. The integration of standardized scoring systems and normative benchmarks, as recommended by neurorehabilitation consortia, can enhance diagnostic accuracy and longitudinal tracking. Future guidelines must also account for subtype-specific manifestations and temporal dynamics, ensuring assessments are sensitive to change over the recovery trajectory.

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Screening and Diagnostic Tools for Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Clinical screening for visuospatial neglect requires standardized, ecologically valid tools that detect deficits across multiple spatial domains—personal, peri-personal, and extra-personal. While traditional paper-and-pencil tests such as line bisection and cancellation tasks remain widely used, their sensitivity is limited to peri-personal space and may miss subtle or modality-specific neglect. Recent normative data for the distal line bisection task, performed with a laser pointer at 3 meters, and the baking tray task provide validated cut-off values for diagnosing unilateral spatial neglect in both experimental and clinical settings, enhancing detection in extra-personal space ref [26]. Systematic screening protocols, as recommended in post-stroke rehabilitation guidelines, have demonstrated that neglect is significantly underdiagnosed in routine clinical practice, with up to 61% of cases undocumented in patient charts despite objective screening ref [25].

To improve diagnostic accuracy, multi-modal batteries combining behavioral, functional, and ecological assessments are increasingly advocated. Tools such as the Catherine Bergego Scale and the Behavioral Inattention Test (BIT) offer structured scoring systems that capture both motor and perceptual components of neglect. Emerging digital adaptations, including tablet-based cancellation tasks and virtual reality paradigms, further enhance sensitivity and objectivity. However, standardization across centers remains inconsistent, underscoring the need for protocol harmonization and routine integration of validated screening tools into acute stroke pathways to optimize rehabilitation planning and long-term outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Evidence from Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review
subsections.subsection_title: Network-Level Effects of Non-invasive Stimulation on Attention Circuits
subsections.content:
Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques, particularly rTMS and TBS, have revealed that attentional networks operate as distributed, interhemispherically balanced systems rather than isolated regions. Inhibitory rTMS applied to the right posterior parietal cortex induces immediate local suppression but triggers delayed, long-range changes in functional connectivity across the dorsal fronto-parietal network, as demonstrated by fMRI studies showing altered interregional synchronization up to 30 minutes post-stimulation ref [27]. These delayed effects underscore the network-level propagation of stimulation-induced perturbations, extending beyond the stimulated site to modulate contralateral homologous regions and frontal attentional control areas.

Theta-band functional connectivity within the dorsal fronto-parietal network has been shown to predict the efficiency of goal-directed attention, suggesting that rhythmic coordination between parietal and frontal nodes is a key mechanism underlying spatial orienting ref [30]. Disruption of this network via theta burst stimulation (TBS) over the right PPC in healthy individuals replicates neglect-like behavioral patterns, including reduced leftward visual exploration and increased rightward fixation bias, confirming the causal role of interhemispheric dynamics in spatial attention ref [6]. Furthermore, multimodal evidence from fMRI and TMS demonstrates that spatial attention is governed by competitive interactions between hemispheres, where each hemisphere generates a contralateral attentional weight that collectively determines behavioral bias ref [7]. These findings collectively support a network-based model of neglect, wherein therapeutic interventions must target distributed circuit dynamics rather than focal lesions.

subsections.section_title: Evidence from Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review
subsections.subsection_title: tDCS Modulation of Parietal Cortex for Attentional Recovery
subsections.content:
Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has emerged as a promising neuromodulatory tool for targeting the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) to ameliorate visuospatial neglect. Anodal tDCS applied over the right PPC enhances cortical excitability, thereby counteracting the hypoactivation typically observed in the damaged hemisphere, while cathodal tDCS over the left PPC suppresses pathological overactivity in the intact hemisphere, restoring interhemispheric balance. A randomized controlled trial demonstrated that both anodal right PPC and cathodal left PPC tDCS significantly improved performance on the motor-free visual perception test, line bisection test, and star cancellation test compared to sham stimulation, suggesting a dual-pathway mechanism of action ref [34]. Similarly, anodal tDCS over the right PPC was shown to improve visual scanning in subacute stroke patients, with significant gains in figure cancellation and line bisection tasks immediately following stimulation ref [7]. These effects are consistent with findings from healthy participants, where biparietal tDCS induced predictable shifts in visuospatial localization, supporting the model of hemispheric competition in spatial attention ref [32].

Beyond single-site stimulation, biparietal tDCS protocols—combining anodal stimulation of the right PPC with cathodal stimulation of the left PPC—have been explored in single-case studies, yielding sustained improvements in neglect symptoms when paired with cognitive training ref [35]. Furthermore, combining tDCS with feedback training enhanced outcomes in subacute stroke patients, with greater improvements in visual perception and functional mobility compared to feedback training alone ref [6]. The temporal dynamics of tDCS effects, including delayed post-stimulation rebound effects observed in healthy subjects, suggest that tDCS may induce neuroplastic changes beyond immediate excitability shifts ref [32]. Collectively, these findings support tDCS modulation of the PPC as a viable, non-invasive adjuvant therapy for attentional recovery in neglect, with effects most robust when integrated with behavioral rehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Evidence from Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review
subsections.subsection_title: Therapeutic Efficacy of rTMS and TBS in Neglect Rehabilitation
subsections.content:
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and theta burst stimulation (TBS) have emerged as promising neuromodulatory interventions for visuospatial neglect, primarily targeting the interhemispheric imbalance hypothesis. Low-frequency rTMS applied to the contralesional posterior parietal cortex has demonstrated significant improvements in neglect symptoms, as shown in a pilot study where 2 weeks of daily stimulation enhanced performance on line cancellation and line bisection tasks ref [38]. Similarly, a randomized controlled trial in acute stroke patients found that 4 weeks of active rTMS led to significantly greater gains in visual perception, line bisection, and cancellation tasks compared to sham stimulation ref [42].

Theta burst stimulation, particularly continuous TBS (cTBS), has shown robust and durable effects. A single session of repeated cTBS over the left parietal cortex improved visual neglect for up to 32 hours, with effects proportional to the number of stimulation trains applied ref [36]. Subsequent studies confirmed that 10-day cTBS protocols significantly enhance behavioral outcomes, with improvements sustained for up to 4 weeks post-treatment ref [9]. These effects are associated with modulation of the dorsal attention network, as evidenced by resting-state fMRI showing reduced pathological connectivity in the right hemisphere following cTBS ref [8].

Importantly, TBS has also translated to functional gains in daily living: repeated cTBS significantly reduced disability as measured by the Catherine Bergego Scale, indicating real-world relevance beyond laboratory tasks ref [41]. Furthermore, intermittent TBS (iTBS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex improved attentional control and functional connectivity, suggesting that stimulation beyond the parietal cortex may also be efficacious ref [40]. Collectively, these findings support rTMS and TBS as viable, mechanism-informed therapies for neglect rehabilitation.

subsections.section_title: Evidence from Non-invasive Brain Stimulation: A Systematic Review
subsections.subsection_title: Interhemispheric Imbalance as a Mechanism in Visuospatial Neglect
subsections.content:
Visuospatial neglect is widely theorized to arise from an interhemispheric imbalance, wherein unilateral brain damage—typically in the right posterior parietal cortex—disrupts the tonic inhibitory interactions between homologous regions in both hemispheres. This leads to pathological hyperexcitability of the intact left hemisphere, which in turn suppresses residual attentional processing in the damaged right hemisphere. Evidence from non-invasive brain stimulation supports this model: cathodal tDCS over the intact parietal cortex or anodal tDCS over the lesioned side both reduce neglect symptoms by rebalancing interhemispheric competition, as demonstrated in both healthy controls and stroke patients ref [44]. Similarly, inhibitory theta burst stimulation (TBS) over the right posterior parietal cortex induces a neglect-like bias in healthy subjects, which is reversed by subsequent TBS over the left parietal cortex, confirming the dynamic, bidirectional nature of this rivalry ref [45]. Functional imaging studies further reveal that rTMS-induced disruption of the right intraparietal sulcus alters interhemispheric fMRI connectivity, directly linking behavioral deficits to disrupted interhemispheric dynamics ref [43].

Critically, hyperexcitability in the intact hemisphere is not merely correlative but causally implicated in neglect persistence. Twin-coil TMS studies have shown enhanced functional connectivity between the left parietal and motor cortices in neglect patients compared to stroke patients without neglect and healthy controls, indicating maladaptive plasticity in the intact hemisphere ref [12]. Moreover, suppressing this hyperactivity via continuous TBS over the left posterior parietal cortex significantly improves neglect severity and normalizes parieto-frontal excitability, supporting the notion that reducing left-hemisphere dominance accelerates recovery ref [11]. Even frontal regions contribute to this imbalance: left frontal TMS reduces contralesional extinction in right-brain-damaged patients, suggesting that interhemispheric competition extends beyond parietal networks to include frontal attentional control systems ref [48]. Together, these findings solidify interhemispheric imbalance as a core pathophysiological mechanism in visuospatial neglect.

subsections.subsection_title: Systematic Reviews of Pharmacological and Therapeutic Approaches
subsections.content:
Systematic reviews of pharmacological interventions for visuospatial neglect (VSN) have consistently highlighted the exploratory nature and methodological limitations of existing clinical trials. A seminal review by van der Kemp et al. (ref [49]) analyzed 11 human studies, revealing that while dopaminergic agents showed mixed outcomes—three reporting benefits and three indicating adverse effects—cholinergic treatments demonstrated more consistent positive effects across multiple outcome measures. Noradrenergic stimulation was found to specifically enhance attentional maintenance during spatial exploration. The review underscored the overall low to moderate methodological quality of included studies, calling for standardized outcome measures and larger randomized controlled trials. Subsequent systematic evaluations have corroborated these findings, noting that pharmacological approaches remain adjunctive rather than curative, with limited generalizability due to heterogeneous patient populations and outcome assessments. Recent meta-analyses have further emphasized the potential of cholinergic modulation, particularly acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, as a promising avenue for future research, given their influence on attentional networks implicated in VSN. However, the lack of long-term follow-up and inconsistent dosing protocols across studies continues to hinder clinical translation.

Beyond dopaminergic, cholinergic, and noradrenergic systems, a few reviews have begun to examine multimodal pharmacological strategies, including combinations with cognitive training or non-invasive brain stimulation. Nevertheless, high-quality systematic evidence remains sparse, and no pharmacological agent has yet achieved guideline-recommended status for VSN. The field urgently requires rigorously designed trials with pre-specified primary endpoints, stratification by neglect subtype, and inclusion of functional outcomes to determine true therapeutic efficacy.

Therapeutic interventions for unilateral neglect demonstrate variable efficacy in improving functional outcomes, with evidence suggesting that reductions in neglect severity often correlate with gains in activities of daily living (ADLs). A systematic review of 37 randomized controlled trials found that while multiple rehabilitation approaches—ranging from bottom-up sensory stimulation to top-down awareness training—yield promising results, the overall level of evidence remains low due to methodological heterogeneity, small sample sizes, and inadequate blinding ref [50]. Functional improvements are most consistently reported when assessments incorporate standardized, multidimensional outcome measures that capture motor, cognitive, and social domains, rather than isolated neuropsychological tests ref [51]. Notably, neglect severity has been identified as an independent predictor of long-term functional disability, particularly in homogeneous right-hemisphere stroke cohorts, underscoring the need for early and comprehensive rehabilitation targeting both spatial and non-spatial attentional deficits ref [51].

Despite advances in neuromodulatory techniques, the generalization of therapeutic gains to real-world functioning remains inconsistent. Studies incorporating longitudinal follow-ups beyond one year are scarce, limiting understanding of sustained functional recovery ref [51]. Moreover, the lack of consensus on optimal outcome measures—such as the integration of ecological tasks like the baking tray or Catherine Bergego Scale—hampers cross-study comparability. Future trials must prioritize large-scale, multicenter designs with blinded assessors, standardized neglect batteries, and functional outcomes anchored in patient-centered goals to establish clinically meaningful efficacy ref [50].

subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacological Interventions Targeting Noradrenergic and Dopaminergic Systems
subsections.content:
Pharmacological interventions targeting noradrenergic and dopaminergic systems have emerged as promising strategies for ameliorating visuospatial neglect, particularly in patients with right-hemisphere stroke. Noradrenergic modulation, via the α2A receptor agonist guanfacine, has been shown to enhance leftward space exploration by improving sustained attention and vigilance, likely through action on the intact dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. In a pivotal study, guanfacine administration led to significant improvements in spatial exploration tasks without altering basic sensory or motor function, supporting the hypothesis that noradrenergic pathways modulate attentional maintenance in neglect ref [52].

Similarly, dopaminergic agents have demonstrated therapeutic potential. A case series using carbidopa-L-dopa in four patients with right-hemisphere stroke reported clinically meaningful improvements in behavioral inattention test scores and functional outcomes on the FIM™, suggesting that dopamine augmentation may restore attentional bias toward the contralesional space ref [53]. Preclinical evidence further supports this approach: in rats with unilateral dorsomedial prefrontal lesions, apomorphine—a dopamine receptor agonist—significantly reduced polymodal neglect behaviors, an effect blocked by dopamine antagonists, implicating dopaminergic circuits in the pathophysiology of neglect ref [4].

Together, these findings underscore the role of monoaminergic systems in attentional control beyond primary sensory-motor deficits. While larger randomized trials are needed, current evidence supports the rationale for targeted noradrenergic and dopaminergic pharmacotherapy as adjuncts to rehabilitation in selected neglect patients.
